newsitem.title: USA: Lower prices to curtail global wheat sowings--USDA.
newsitem.headline: Lower prices to curtail global wheat sowings--USDA.

text.p: Lower market prices will constrain wheat sowings by U.S. competitors but there will be little chance for U.S. exports to rise in 1997/98, Agriculture Department economists said Monday.

"Unlike 1996/97, U.S. competitors will enter the 1997/98 marketing year with large stocks, providing intense competition for U.S. exporters," USDA's Economic Research Service said in its Wheat Yearbook.
"Dramatically lower prices in 1996/97 are expected to curtail acreage planted to wheat in foreign exporting countries, especially Canada, Australia and Argentina."
Nonetheless, the yearbook said, the major exporting nations "will carry large stocks into the new marketing year and only moderate import growth is expected."

At its Outlook Forum last week, USDA projected a U.S. wheat crop of 2.27 billion bushels, slightly less than 1996's 2.28 billion, and 1997/98 exports of one billion bushels, compared to the forecast 950 million for 1996/97.

U.S. wheat supplies in 1996/97 were expected to be the lowest since 1976/77 due to small beginning stocks and poor winter wheat output. Average farm-gate price was forecast for $4.20-$4.40 per bushel, down from the record highs established in early 1996 when global wheat supplies were short.
Growing conditions in the Northern Hemisphere for the new crop have been mixed, USDA said. Europe experienced extreme cold but snowfall should prevent winterkill in many areas.
Morocco and Spain have received favorable moisture amounts but Tunisia and Algeria have been drier than usual. Weather has been normal in China and India.

USDA has projected 70 million acres would be sown with wheat for harvest this year, compared to 75.6 million acres last year. In January, USDA reported 48.3 million acres were sown to winter wheat, down three million from 1996 and the smallest area since 1978.
